name: Hausa
variant: Standard (Kano) Hausa of northern Nigeria, written in Latin (boko) script
script: Latin (boko) with extra letters: ɓ, ɗ, ƙ and 'y; tone and vowel length are not written in everyday spelling; left to right
basis: Peace Corps Niger, An Introduction to the Hausa Language (2006, 24 lessons): pronunciation, greetings and everyday expressions, days and time, numbers and money, food, prices and question words, then 'to be' with ne / ce and its negative, the -na (continuous) forms and da for 'have', future, past and past negative
src: Peace Corps Niger, An Introduction to the Hausa Language (April 2006), table of contents, lessons 1-24 (opened as a PDF through a web reader)
note: Only the Peace Corps Niger course gave an order, and it teaches the Hausa of Niger. The Kano / Nigerian standard is taught here instead: the hooked letters ɓ ɗ ƙ 'y, naira and kobo, and every Hausa form in the titles are from my own knowledge, not from the source. The survival topics (greetings, days and time, numbers, money, prices and question words, food) come from the source, but their order is mine: question words before numbers, money and time, and food moved to the last stage. The grammar the source covers keeps its order (ne / ce, negative ba … ba, the -na forms with da for 'have', future, past, past negative), except that ne / ce moves to the first stage so that introductions can use it. Other Hausa course pages I opened (HAUSA 1010 on abu-ubaida.com, Wisconsin, Harvard ALP, UC Press, the FSI Hausa Basic Course PDF) gave no usable lesson order. Gender, possession, the subjunctive and commands, plurals, adjectives with mai, family and directions are not in the source and are placed by common course practice and my own judgment. The source's weather lesson is left out to keep 25 lessons; the split into lessons and stages is my own.
hardest: Tone and vowel length change meaning but are not written in ordinary spelling
The hooked (glottalized) consonants ɓ, ɗ, ƙ and 'y next to plain b, d, k, y
Grammatical gender everywhere: kai / ke for 'you', ne / ce for 'is', -n / -r linkers
Tense and aspect carried by the pronoun, not the verb (ina zuwa, na zo, zan zo), and irregular plurals

items: ha-sounds
Sounds and spelling: the hooked letters ɓ, ɗ, ƙ and 'y, and ts, sh, c
ha-tones
Tone and vowel length: heard in every word, but not written in everyday spelling
ha-greetings
Greetings: Sannu, Ina kwana?, Lafiya lau, Barka da yamma
ha-courtesy
Thanks and leave-taking: Na gode, Sai an jima, Sai gobe
ha-ne-ce
Pronouns and 'is': ni, kai, ke, shi, ita, mu, ku, su with ne and ce
ha-intro
Introducing yourself: Sunana…, Ina sunanka?, Ni Ba'amurke ne
ha-gender
Masculine and feminine nouns (yaro / yarinya) and this / that: wannan, wancan
ha-possession
Possession: the linkers -n and -r, and endings like sunana, gidana, motata
ha-negative-is
'Is not': ba … ba ne / ba … ba ce (Ba malami ba ne)
ha-questions
Question words: me, wa, ina, yaushe, nawa, yaya, and ko for yes/no
ha-numbers
Numbers: ɗaya, biyu, uku … goma, ashirin, ɗari, dubu
ha-money
Money, prices and bargaining: Nawa ne?, naira, kobo
ha-time
Days and time: yau, gobe, jiya; Litinin, Talata; ƙarfe nawa?
ha-continuous
The continuous: ina, kana, kina, yana, tana (Ina karatu); being somewhere (Yana gida)
ha-da
Having with da: Ina da mota, Ba ni da kuɗi
ha-continuous-neg
Negative continuous: ba na, ba ka, ba ya (Ba na so)
ha-completive
The completive (past): na, ka, kin, ya, ta, mun, kun, sun (Ya tafi)
ha-completive-neg
Negative past with ba … ba: Ban gani ba, Bai zo ba
ha-future
Future: zan, za ka, zai, za ta (Zan tafi gobe)
ha-subjunctive
Commands and the subjunctive: zo, ka zauna, mu tafi, don Allah
ha-food
Food and ordering: Ina son…, abinci, ruwa, shayi, tuwo
ha-family
Family: uba, uwa, ɗan'uwa, 'yar'uwa, miji, mata
ha-plurals
Plurals in many patterns: yaro / yara, mota / motoci, gida / gidaje
ha-describing
Describing: babba, ƙarami, sabo, and mai (mai kyau)
ha-directions
Directions: hagu, dama, gaba, kusa, nesa
